title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
author: jasondavies
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
textRawHtml: Related: Levent Alpöge claims proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis [pdf] - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50574968
textZhHtml: Related: Levent Alpöge claims proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis [pdf] - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50574968
summaryRaw: The story so far: Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it was so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current version, in the state that it happens to be in (mid-revision). Yesterday, in the midst of meetings, I hurriedly posted it, writing: “I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is.”

About 8 hours later I updated: “I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)”
Links (including the draft), at which further updates can hopefully be found: John Baez and Álvaro Lozano-Robledo.

This will probably be my final update on the subject, barring major new developments. For future questions about the mathematics, please contact Brian Conrad; I haven’t yet had the chance even to look at Masullo’s document, having just received it Friday (and in any case, it is out of my expertise). These are exciting times, and I look forward to the acceleration of mathematical discovery continuing!

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.textRawHtml:
The manuscript claims he has been working on this problem for 12 years. I can only imagine the feelings that must have hit him when he saw the Anthropic announcement. Though if he believed he had solved it, he must have known it was only a matter of time until one of the AI companies found it, too.

A hurried announcement with the draft published within hours is the only way to claim a tie to the discovery. Time will tell if either holds up under further analysis, but at least he has shown his hand to the world with a timestamp on it now.

children.author: nilkn
children.textRawHtml:
I've been thinking about what I'd do if I were in this situation.

Keep it tight and have a few trusted mathematicians review? You're at the risk of Anthropic throwing millions of dollars and internal models at it and beating you, which is exactly what Levent just did.

Try to formalize it yourself? You can't, because that would cost millions of dollars at this scale. Your university system can't afford that, and if you give a lab even a hint of how you did it they'll scoop you immediately.

Just dump it out in public, knowing it's not fully reviewed, hasn't been formalized, and could contain a fatal mistake? Anyone sharing an unverified proof of something as legendary as Riemann, spread over nearly 1,000 pages, would not necessarily be taken seriously, especially after the ABC fiasco. People have been doing this for 100+ years. You'd also just be giving fuel to the labs to build on and potentially take credit away from you if you did actually nearly have a solution.

What was the winning strategy? Or was there none? Perhaps letting a lab burn massive compute on a formal solution, then releasing your attempt same day, really was the optimal strategy.

children.author: palata
children.textRawHtml:
> An interesting strategy

Is it, though?

As a developer, before AI, I took pride in solving challenging problems. I could show them and say: "this was hard, but I persisted and I solved it". Not that they would change the world, but it was obvious that they were challenging.

AI completely changed that: even if I now solved such a problem "manually", people will just assume that it wasn't that hard now that we have AI. Do I want to be the guy who really insists on saying that "no, no, I promise, I solved it on my own"? Then others will just think "yeah you wasted time, you could have used AI".

I believe it may be the same for Masullo: he worked on that for 12 years. If now he partners with an AI company, people will just think "sure, he failed at it for 12 years, and now AI solved it for him". I think he's screwed anyway: even if his current proof is correct (or almost correct), people can assume he quickly finished it with AI. I have never worked on a challenging problem for 12 years, I can only imagine how hard it would be to have it destroyed by AI.

I don't think anyone can "discover" anything today and get the same kind of credit they would have 5 years ago. AI broke that, period.

children.author: cmcclellan
children.textRawHtml:
I was a bit young when search engines emerged, but I can imagine a similar feeling. Information suddenly became a commodity, which probably felt really demoralizing for very knowledgeable people. Answer a question well and someone could just say “oh you just searched that”.

We are still early in the AI age, but I can imagine there will be a lot of disruption at first, but eventually things will settle down and humans will find out their new roles.

children.author: palata
children.textRawHtml:
I think it is different in the sense that knowledge is still valuable. When you interact with a human being in real life, your knowledge is useful. And if you know many things, you can reason about them.

For development, before AI it was already hard to explain to e.g. a manager why something that looks easy is hard, and something that looks hard is actually easy. But what they could observe was that the more experienced developers were able to solve problems that the less experienced ones weren't. The value was "we had to ask this guy because the juniors were struggling".

With AI, a lot of this disappears. In many cases the manager does not even need the junior to vibe code something that looks like it works.

Also with AI, a lot of the developer job seems to be "an AI did the fun part of building something, and I need to do the boring part of reviewing, maintaining and being responsible for it". It makes me more productive by removing the fun and challenging parts and leaving me the boring ones.

children.author: thesz
children.textRawHtml:
From the software engineering perspective, the fun part is where you can introduce defects into the code. The main process of gaining experience is to get knowledge how and get oneself able not to introduce errors into the code.

With the removal of the fun part, you also removed the part that you can improve by yourself.

children.author: thomquaid
children.textRawHtml: It became obvious to me as a Math kid in University that RH would fall in my lifetime, and that I didnt have the tools for the project, and probably never would in time to be the one to publish the result. I have enormous respect for the 12 years Alessandro Masulli put in on this project, which seems like a Hero's task to me. My biggest fear, essentially, could be distilled down to what just happened to Alessandro. If I was Mr Masullo, I would hope to have the courage to immediatly publish the draft magnum opus. To think it is all gone in a moment is too heartbreaking not to hear a clarion call to action. I commend him and respect his incredible courage and dedication to this great Reinmann problem. Humanity has advanced its frontiers today, permanently.
